## Charter

# CHARTER — Off-Peak Fare Capping at Riverton Transit Authority: A Briefing Note

## Deliverable
What: A briefing note to the Riverton Transit Authority (RTA) Board of
Directors evaluating whether RTA should adopt an off-peak fare cap, and
recommending how. Through-line: RTA should adopt an off-peak fare cap
through a phased, corridor-first pilot, because peer-agency evidence shows
off-peak capping grows ridership without a full-fare-equivalent revenue
loss, and RTA's own ridership and equity data show the riders most
underserved by its current all-day cap are exactly the riders concentrated
in the off-peak window.
Format: markdown, rendered last via the format skill
Total size: 4200w, 5items
(body sections only, B002-B006; the executive summary is front-matter.md and
the conclusion/recommendation is back-matter.md, written by hand in the seam
pass — see PLAN.md and WALKTHROUGH.md — and are not separately budgeted plan
units)

## Audience
The RTA Board of Directors and the General Manager's senior staff. They know
RTA's network and current fare structure well; they do not have the peer-
agency data, the fare-system technical constraints, or the equity office's
analysis in front of them, and this note is their first consolidated look at
all three together ahead of a vote on whether to direct staff to proceed.

## Voice & register
Third person, board-briefing register: precise, plain, comfortable citing
figures, and willing to name a tradeoff without hiding it. No first person,
no rhetorical questions, and no recommendation stated as settled until the
conclusion — body sections lay out evidence and tradeoffs, not verdicts.

## Non-negotiables
1. Every ridership, revenue, cost, or date figure carries a [S#] source tag
   traceable to a file in Sources of truth.
2. The terminology lock is followed exactly; no synonyms for locked terms.
3. The implementation options section presents at least two options as
   options the Board could choose among, never as a decision already made.
4. Equity implications for low-income riders are addressed as their own
   subject, not folded into a general accessibility statement.
5. No section before the conclusion states outright that RTA should adopt
   an off-peak cap; sections build the evidence, the conclusion states the
   recommendation.

### batches/B003.md

## 2. RTA Ridership and Revenue by Time of Day

RTA recorded 21.4 million boardings systemwide in FY2026, up 1.8% from
FY2025, and $28.6 million in fixed-route fare revenue [S2]. RTA has run a
single fare product since 2019 [S2]: an all-day cap under which a rider
pays full fare for their first two taps in a service day, 6:00 a.m.-11:59
p.m., and rides free the rest of that day no matter when those first two
taps happen [S2]. That design mechanically rewards a specific travel
pattern. A rider who taps twice during the morning commute reaches the cap
on the commute alone and then rides free for any trip later that day,
including an evening or weekend trip; a rider whose only trips fall outside
the morning commute never reaches the cap on those trips and pays full fare
for each one [S2]. The cap, in other words, is time-blind by design but not
time-blind in effect: it pays off fastest for a peak-anchored, multi-trip
rider and offers nothing extra to a rider whose travel is concentrated later
in the day, however many separate trips that rider makes.

This matters against the peer-agency findings in Section 1. Meridian and
Cedar Falls both built their off-peak cap on top of an existing account-based
fare product much like RiverPass; RTA's own all-day cap is exactly that kind
of product, already in place and already capable of being read at the point
of a tap. The open question Section 1 could not answer on its own is
whether RTA's riders are actually distributed across the day in a way that
would make a second, off-peak-specific cap worth building. The day-part data
below answers that question directly.

RTA's own fare-collection system divides each service day into three
day-parts for reporting: AM peak (6:00-9:30 a.m.), daytime (9:30 a.m.-6:30
p.m., which folds in the PM peak, 4:00-6:30 p.m.), and off-peak (6:30
p.m.-11:59 p.m., plus all weekend hours) [S2]. In FY2026, AM peak
accounted for 6.2 million boardings, 29% of the system total, and $9.1
million in revenue [S2]. Daytime accounted for 10.5 million boardings, 49%
of the total, and $13.8 million in revenue [S2]. Off-peak accounted for 4.7
million boardings, 22% of the total, and $5.7 million in revenue [S2].
Average revenue per boarding is highest in AM peak, at $1.47, and lowest
off-peak, at $1.21 [S2] — a gap the all-day cap's mechanics explain directly:
RTA Planning estimates 38% of off-peak boardings are made by riders who had
already reached the cap earlier the same day and are riding for no
incremental revenue at all, while the remaining 62% are riders making an
off-peak-only trip, or a second trip on a day when their first trip was also
off-peak, and so paying full fare with no cap benefit either way [S2].

Off-peak ridership is also RTA's fastest-growing segment: it rose 3.1% year
over year, against 1.8% growth system-wide, driven mostly by evening service
on RTA's two light-rail lines [S2]. That growth has not run into a capacity
constraint. RTA's fleet-utilization data shows off-peak trips running at 34%
average seat occupancy system-wide, compared with 78% in AM peak and 71% in
PM peak, and no route in the FY2026 schedule is capacity-constrained during
off-peak hours [S2]. Whatever ridership response an off-peak-specific cap
produced, RTA's existing off-peak service already has the seats to carry it
without adding trips or altering the current evening and weekend schedule
RTA already runs.

RTA has changed its fare structure twice in recent history: the current
all-day cap was introduced in 2019, and the base fare itself was last
increased by $0.15 in 2021 [S2]. Both changes went through a 90-day public
comment period under RTA's fare-change policy, and neither introduced a
product differentiated by time of day — the all-day cap has applied
uniformly regardless of when a rider's first two taps occur since it began
[S2]. RTA has not previously operated a fare product that treats an evening
or weekend trip differently from a morning or midday one, which is the gap
an off-peak-specific cap would be the first RTA product to close. Whether
that gap matters most for revenue, for ridership, or for which riders it
reaches is a question the day-part figures above only partly answer, since
a boardings-and-revenue breakdown by time of day says nothing on its own
about which riders make up each of those three day-parts or why. The
equity implications of who is actually riding in each of these day-parts,
and how well RTA's current all-day cap serves them, are taken up next.

### sources/equity-analysis-notes.md

# Equity office analysis notes — off-peak ridership and low-income riders

Prepared by RTA's Equity & Access office, 2026-08, using FY2026 reduced-fare
program enrollment as a proxy for low-income ridership (RTA does not collect
rider income directly; reduced-fare enrollment requires documented enrollment
in one of four qualifying income-based assistance programs).

## Enrollment and travel pattern

RTA's reduced-fare program has 41,000 enrolled riders as of FY2026. Enrolled
riders account for 19% of system-wide boardings but 33% of off-peak
boardings — reduced-fare riders are roughly twice as likely, proportionally,
to be traveling off-peak as the ridership base overall. The Equity office's
working explanation, drawn from a FY2025 rider survey, is that enrolled
riders disproportionately work evening, overnight, or weekend shifts in
retail, food service, and healthcare support roles, and disproportionately
make non-work trips (grocery, medical, childcare pickup) outside the
traditional 9-to-5 travel window that the current all-day cap was designed
around.

## Why the current all-day cap underserves this group

Because RTA's existing all-day cap only pays off once a rider has already
taken 2 taps that day, it mechanically benefits multi-trip peak-anchored
travel most: a rider who commutes in and out during peak hours reaches the
cap on their commute alone and then rides free the rest of the day, including
any off-peak trips. A rider whose only trips that day are off-peak — the
pattern the Equity office's survey associates most with enrolled reduced-fare
riders — pays full fare for both taps and never reaches the cap at all. The
Equity office's analysis states plainly that the current fare structure's
largest cap benefit accrues to peak commuters, not to the reduced-fare
population the program exists to serve.

## Geographic concentration

Reduced-fare enrollment is concentrated in four of RTA's twelve service
corridors (the Eastside, Harbor, Millbrook, and Southgate corridors), which
together account for 58% of all enrolled riders despite carrying 31% of
system-wide boardings. All four of these corridors also appear in RTA's
off-peak ridership growth data as above-average growth corridors over the
past two years. The Equity office notes this overlap as suggestive, not
proven: it has not run a corridor-level regression isolating the reduced-fare
population's contribution to each corridor's off-peak growth.

## What an off-peak cap could change

An off-peak-specific cap — one that pays off after fewer taps than the
current all-day cap, but only for taps in the off-peak window — would create
a path to fare relief for a rider whose only travel that day is off-peak,
which the current structure does not. The Equity office's preliminary
estimate, based on applying Meridian Transit's reported 11% off-peak
ridership response to RTA's reduced-fare-heavy corridors only, is that
enrolled riders in the four highest-concentration corridors could see
off-peak trip costs fall by an amount comparable to Cedar Falls Regional
Transit's reported outcome for its enrolled population, though the Equity
office is explicit that this is an extrapolation from two peer agencies, not
a Riverton-specific model.

## Caution the office asked to be carried forward

The Equity office's notes ask explicitly that any proposal be evaluated
against whether it also serves non-enrolled low-income riders — people who
would qualify for reduced fare but have not completed enrollment — since a
cap benefit tied only to enrollment status would miss a share of the
population the equity goal is meant to reach; the office did not estimate
the size of that unenrolled-but-eligible group in this analysis.
